title: Earth_Lusca_Incident_Response_a78
description: Investigate and respond to a potential Earth Lusca malware compromise involving the KTLVdoor backdoor.
outcomes: Investigation of systemd services and configuration files

levels.title: Introduction
levels.content: The organization has detected unusual network activity potentially related to the Earth Lusca malware family, specifically the KTLVdoor backdoor. Your team has been tasked with investigating and responding to this potential compromise. During this investigation, you will encounter various types of flags, including port numbers and file paths.

levels.title: Get Access
levels.cloud_content:

- Host: target (192.168.50.5)

To proceed to the next level, enter the word 'start'.
levels.local_content:

- Password: cyrano

To proceed to the next level, enter the word 'start'.

levels.title: Investigate Suspicious Network Activity
levels.content: While monitoring network traffic, you've noticed unusual outbound connections from the target host. Investigate this activity to identify any suspicious services or processes that might be responsible. The suspicious service is running on port 443 (port number).
levels.solution: Check running services and network connections to identify any unusual activity. Use commands like netstat -tuln, ss -tuln, or lsof -i to identify the suspicious service.

hints.title: Conceptual Hint
hints.content: Start by understanding the types of network connections that are established from the host.

hints.title: Methodological Hint
hints.content: Use network monitoring tools to list all active network connections and listening ports.

hints.title: Command Hint
hints.content: Try using the command 'netstat -tuln' to list all active network connections and listening ports.

levels.title: Analyze Persistence Mechanism
levels.content: Now that you've identified the suspicious service, determine how it maintains persistence on the system. Investigate startup mechanisms and configuration files to understand how the service is automatically started. The systemd service unit file responsible for the suspicious service's persistence is located at /etc/systemd/system/bkd.service (file path).
levels.solution: Examine systemd services and configuration files to find persistence mechanisms. Use commands like systemctl list-unit-files --type=service, ls /etc/systemd/system, and cat /etc/systemd/system/bkd.service to investigate the persistence mechanism.

hints.title: Conceptual Hint
hints.content: Understand how services can be configured to start automatically on a Linux system.

hints.title: Methodological Hint
hints.content: Look for systemd service unit files that define how services are started and managed.

hints.title: Command Hint
hints.content: Use the command 'systemctl list-unit-files --type=service' to list all systemd service unit files.

levels.title: Investigate Lateral Movement
levels.content: Examine the target host for evidence of lateral movement. Look for any file transfers, remote command execution, or other indicators that the attacker might be moving to other systems within the network. The payload-transfer service and its associated timer, which are used for lateral movement, are located at /etc/systemd/system/payload-transfer.service (file path) and /etc/systemd/system/payload-transfer.timer.
levels.solution: Check for any scheduled tasks, cron jobs, or other mechanisms that might facilitate lateral movement. Use commands like systemctl list-timers, ls /etc/systemd/system, cat /etc/systemd/system/payload-transfer.service, and cat /etc/systemd/system/payload-transfer.timer to investigate lateral movement.

hints.title: Conceptual Hint
hints.content: Understand how attackers can move laterally within a network using scheduled tasks or timers.

hints.title: Methodological Hint
hints.content: Look for systemd timers and services that might be used to schedule tasks or transfer files.

hints.title: Command Hint
hints.content: Use the command 'systemctl list-timers' to list all systemd timers.
